newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee firms as buyers hunt for beans.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee firms as buyers hunt for beans.

text.p: Indonesian coffee prices firmed on Monday, with some buyers venturing to highland growing areas to hunt for beans as supply tightened, traders said.
They said the discount between the export price and London exchange's benchmark September contract had narrowed to around $150, compared with the usual $200 and sometimes $250 discount.

"Some sellers are asking for premiums to the London terminal," one foreign buyer said. "Although the premium prices asked by some can be disregarded as being unrealistic, the discount to the terminal has generally narrowed significantly."
"This is an indication of tight supply," he added. "Although seeking a premium to London prices is an exaggeration of the supply tightness, there seems to be a genuine shortage."

The traders said grade four robusta coffee was quoted at 3,900-4,000 rupiah/kg in the key growing region of Lampung in south Sumatra, compared with 3,800-3,850 rupiah a week ago. The export price was quoted at $1,630/tonne against $1,600-$1,650.
They said some sellers were quoting the export price at $1,650 and as high as $1,700.
London's September contract ended $16 down at $1,785 last Friday despite light roaster buying.

"The local price has remained firm despite the erratic market in London," one trader said. "Sellers are maintaining high local prices because they feel the market will be running out of beans over the next two months."
The trader said some exporters have been buying actively in a bid to build up inventories in anticipation of the supply situation in Indonesia lifting London prices.
"Some big players are continuing to buy beans because they feel the crunch is going to come in a month or two," he said. "They are quietly bullish about prices."
Another trader said some buyers had been heading to the highlands to secure beans directly from the farmers in a bid to fill contracts and build stocks.
"Some of them have been going up-country to get the beans," the trader said. "They are buying aggressively," he added.
Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters (AICE), said early this month that 1997 production was expected to plunge by 160,000 tonnes to 290,000 tonnes from 1996.
He said exportable volume was expected to be around 180,000 tonnes in 1997 against 330,000 in 1996.
